title: Cost and Governance: Finding Waste and Risk
intro: At a large company the cloud bill is a top-five expense, and 'what are we paying for, and who owns it?' is a DevOps question. These commands find the usual waste (orphaned disks, idle IPs, untagged resources) and pull security findings, the same kind of weekly hygiene big platform teams automate.

steps.prompt: Show last month's cost (2026-08-01 to 2026-09-01) grouped by service.
expected_commands: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-08-01,End=2026-09-01 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE
steps.fake_output:
Service                               Amount (USD)
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute  41,210.33
EC2 - Other                             18,904.12
Amazon Relational Database Service      12,488.90
Amazon Simple Storage Service            6,302.45
Amazon Virtual Private Cloud             4,117.80
steps.explanation: Compute is the largest item, but 'EC2 - Other' at almost $19k is suspicious.
steps.why: 'EC2 - Other' is where EBS volumes, snapshots, NAT gateway data processing and data transfer hide. It's frequently the biggest surprise on a bill. Grouping by USAGE_TYPE instead of SERVICE shows which of those it is.

steps.prompt: Find EBS volumes that aren't attached to any instance (status 'available').
steps.fake_output:
VolumeId                Size  Type  CreateTime            Tags
vol-0a11b22c33d44e556   500   gp3   2025-03-02T10:14:00Z  Name=old-es-data-1
vol-0b22c33d44e55f667   500   gp3   2025-03-02T10:14:00Z  Name=old-es-data-2
vol-0c33d44e55f660778   2000  io2   2024-11-20T08:00:00Z  (no tags)
steps.explanation: 3TB of detached disks, one of them expensive io2 with no tags, idle for months.
steps.why: Terminating an instance doesn't always delete its data volumes (DeleteOnTermination is false for extra volumes by default), so they pile up and bill forever. Snapshot anything you might need, confirm with the owner, then delete. The untagged one is exactly why tagging policies exist.

steps.prompt: Find Elastic IPs that aren't associated with anything.
steps.why: AWS now charges for every public IPv4 address, attached or not, so idle ones are pure waste. The JMESPath filter [?AssociationId==null] is a handy pattern: 'show me the things that point at nothing'.

steps.prompt: Find every resource tagged team=data, across all services.
steps.explanation: 38 resources belong to the data team.
steps.why: The tagging API searches across services in one call, which is how cost allocation and 'who owns this?' work at scale. Enforce required tags (owner, team, environment) with tag policies or SCPs at creation time, because retro-tagging thousands of resources never happens.

steps.prompt: Pull the CRITICAL findings from Security Hub.
steps.fake_output:
Title                                                        Resource
S3 general purpose buckets should block public access        arn:aws:s3:::acme-exports
Security groups should not allow ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to 22 sg-0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8
IAM root user access key should not exist                    AWS::::Account:111122223333
steps.explanation: Three critical findings, all misconfigurations rather than exotic attacks.
steps.why: Security Hub gathers GuardDuty, Inspector, and configuration checks (the CIS and AWS Foundational benchmarks) in one place. Notice what's at the top: public buckets, open SSH, root keys. Basic hygiene prevents most cloud breaches, and the security category goes deeper.
